title: Print Immutable Linked List in Reverse
statement:
You get the head of a singly linked list that can be neither changed nor looked inside. A node offers exactly two methods: `printValue()`, which prints that node's value, and `getNext()`, which returns the node after it, or `null` after the last node. Write `printLinkedListInReverse(head)` so that it prints the value of every node exactly once, starting with the last node and finishing with the first. Only these two methods may be used: values and links cannot be read directly, and the list cannot be altered. The function returns nothing.

Each case is written as `[head]`: the list's values from the first node to the last. The judge builds the immutable nodes from it and passes your function the first one. The result is the sequence of values your `printValue()` calls produced, in the order they were made.
constraints: The list has between 1 and 1000 nodes
Nodes can only be used through printValue() and getNext()
api: printLinkedListInReverse(head: ImmutableListNode): void, with interface ImmutableListNode { printValue(): void; getNext(): ImmutableListNode | null }
notes:
## Intuition

The list can only be walked forwards, yet the values must come out backwards. That is exactly what a stack is for: whatever goes in last comes out first. Walk the list once, pushing each node, then pop the nodes one by one and print each as it comes off. If extra memory were not allowed, you could instead count the nodes and, for each position from the last to the first, walk from the head to that position and print it: O(1) space but O(n²) time.

## Approach

1. Create an empty `stack` and start `node` at `head`.
2. While `node` is not `null`, push it and move to `node.getNext()`.
3. While the stack is not empty, pop the `top` node and call `top.printValue()`.

The last node pushed is the list's tail, so it is printed first, and the head is printed last.

## Example 1, step by step

`head = [1, 2, 3, 4]`. The first loop pushes the nodes holding 1, 2, 3 and 4, then `getNext()` on the last node returns `null` and the loop stops. The second loop pops 4, 3, 2 and 1 in that order and prints each, so the printed sequence is `[4, 3, 2, 1]`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n): every node is pushed once and popped once.
- Space: O(n): the stack holds every node at once.

## Pitfalls

- Push the node objects, not values: a value can only be produced by calling `printValue()` on its node.
- Stop when `getNext()` returns `null`; calling a method on `null` throws.
- Print each node exactly once; printing during the first walk as well would add the values in forward order too.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `stack` | the nodes visited so far, last one on top |
| `node` | the node the forward walk is at |
| `top` | the node just popped, printed next |

narration.2: The stack will hold every node, with the most recent one on top.
narration.3: Begin the forward walk at the head.
narration.5: Keep walking until we step past the last node.
narration.7: Move to the following node; getNext returns null after the tail.
narration.10: Now unwind: the stack gives the nodes back in reverse order.
narration.11: Take the most recently pushed node, which is the latest one not yet printed.
narration.12: Print its value: the tail comes out first and the head last.
